newsitem.title: UK: Full text of July UK Purchasing Managers' survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of July UK Purchasing Managers' survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the July Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply. The survey is sponsored by Reuters.
Manufacturing expansion continues but export demand falls sharply. Input prices fall at fastest rate since CIPS survey began.

UK purchasing managers reported expansion in manufacturing activity for the fourteenth successive month in July. The seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers' Index fell marginally in the month but remained well above the 'no change' level of 50.0.

The continued expansion of the manufacturing economy largely reflected a strong rise in output during the month. The rate of growth of output accelerated in July as companies reported rising backlogs of orders and further growth in new orders.

Order books strengthened for the fourteenth consecutive month, with consumer driven domestic demand once more the principal source of new business. The pace of growth slowed slightly, however, as export orders fell for the first time since this survey began monitoring exports in January 1996. This decline was almost entirely attributed to the rise in the value of the pound eroding the competitiveness of UK goods overseas.

The continued strength of the pound also continued to reduce the cost of imported goods. Average input prices recorded the sharpest monthly fall since the survey began in July 1991, with almost one in three firms reporting a reduction in average prices compared to the previous month.

Despite falling raw material prices, panel members stressed the need to reduce costs as much as possible in order to maintain competitiveness. The amount of goods purchased rose only modestly, allowing stocks to fall sharply and thereby reduce costs. Stocks of finished goods also fell, again a result of stock reduction policies designed to improve efficiency.

The need to reduce costs was also reflected in employment. Although employment rose for the thirteenth consecutive month, growth was more muted than in previous months as an increasing number of firms were found to have released employees as a result of weakened export order books.

* The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The seasonally adjusted output index rose in July, signalling the fourteenth consecutive monthly increase in output and an acceleration in the rate of growth. Production was again raised in response to further growth in order books. The strongest rise was reported in the production of consumer goods.
NEW ORDERS

The New Orders Index signalled growth for the fourteenth successive month in July with consumer driven domestic demand once more the principal source of new business. Almost one quarter of all companies reported a strengthening of order books during the month but, with export demand contracting significantly, the rate of growth fell to the lowest level recorded since June 1996.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The seasonally adjusted Quantity of Purchases Index rose in July to 52.4. However, the rate of growth of materials purchased remained subdued relative to output growth as firms kept stock levels under control for cost considerations. The index has now recorded growth for seven successive months as manufacturers have increased their purchases of raw materials to satisfy rising production requirements.
PRICES

The seasonally adjusted Prices Index fell sharply in July to record its lowest level since the survey began in July 1991. Almost 30% of companies reported a reduction in prices compared with the previous month, as further appreciation of the pound reduced the cost of imported raw materials. The successful negotiation of lower input prices with suppliers was also widely reported by purchasing managers in July.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The Suppliers' Delivery Times Index fell to its lowest level for over two years in July providing the first significant evidence of supply bottlenecks within the manufacturing sector since the summer of 1995. However, the proportion of firms reporting a lengthening of lead times remains relatively low at 12%. The vast majority of firms reported no change compared to one month ago.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

Purchasing managers reported a further fall in the stocks of purchases held in July. A quarter of all companies reduced stock holdings, choosing to run warehouses as efficiently as possible for cost considerations. A favourable outlook for input prices also reduced the need to hold safety stocks.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Stocks of finished goods fell again in July, with the seasonally adjusted index recording an identical level to June. The implementation of stock reduction policies was once more widely reported by purchasing managers in July, as rising demand was increasingly met from inventories. The Stocks of Finished Goods Index has now fallen for twenty-one months in succession.
EMPLOYMENT

Manufacturing employment rose for the thirteenth consecutive month in July as companies once more recruited staff to satisfy increased production requirements. The rate of growth recorded was slower than in previous months, however, as an increasing number of firms were found to have cut employment levels as a direct result of weak export orders slowing demand.
CONSUMER GOODS

The Output Index for the consumer goods industries recorded by far the greatest monthly rise of all three sectors in July, reaching its highest level since November 1996. Strengthening order books (largely domestically driven) encouraged firms to expand capacity. Following a marked fall in June, consumer goods industries significantly increased their quantity of purchases in July to satisfy the higher production requirements. The sharp increase in demand for raw materials provoked a significant lengthening of suppliers' delivery times, but input prices continued to fall, largely as a result of the deflationary effect of the strength of the pound. Employment fell for the first time since March, however, as producers continued to focus on keeping costs as low as possible.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS

The New Orders Index for investment goods industries indicated further strong growth in July. Buoyant domestic demand was once more the principal source of new business as export orders fell marginally for the first time since May 1996. Output also rose, but at a slower rate than in previous months as manufacturers increasingly chose to satisfy new orders from existing stock levels. Stocks of finished goods have now fallen for twenty-one consecutive months. The deceleration in output growth led to a corresponding slowdown in growth of quantity of purchases. With demand slackening, purchasing managers reported only a marginal lengthening of suppliers delivery times. Input prices, however, fell to their lowest level for six months.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

Both output and new orders of intermediate goods industries recorded strong gains in July, with the Output Index indicating an acceleration in growth. The rate of growth of orders fell, however, as the strength of the pound continued to hit export demand, prompting a fall in overseas orders. The quantity of raw materials purchased by firms increased to meet rising production requirements, but the pace of growth remained relatively subdued. A sharp fall in input prices partly reflected the muted demand for raw materials, but resulted principally from the reduction in import prices caused by the strong pound. Suppliers' delivery times lengthened further in the month. Employment rose for the third consecutive month but continued to lag behind output growth.
NEW EXPORT ORDERS INDEX

The seasonally adjusted new export orders index fell sharply in July, signalling the first decline in export demand since this survey began monitoring exports in January 1996. Over one quarter of all purchasing managers reported a deterioration in export order books compared with the previous month. The decline was almost entirely attributed to the rise in the value of the pound which has eroded the competitiveness of UK goods overseas.
